chapter_title: Introduction to Solidity and Basic Structure

screens.title: Introduction to Solidity and Basic Structure
screens.subtitle: Why Solidity matters, how a contract is structured, and a first working example

narration.text: Today you'll begin learning Solidity, the contract-oriented language used to build smart contracts on Ethereum. Solidity is statically typed and designed to express business logic that runs on the Ethereum Virtual Machine, and that design leads to three core realities you must internalize: every operation costs gas, deployed code is immutable, and state is persisted on-chain. We'll start by explaining the small but essential pieces that make up any contract: the pragma directive that pins compiler compatibility, the contract block that encapsulates state and functions, basic value types like unsigned integers and addresses, and the constructor used at deployment. You'll also see a simple HelloWorld contract that stores and returns a message so you can connect syntax to behavior. As you learn, pay special attention to visibility and the 'view' keyword because they affect who can read state and whether operations require transactions. By the end of this lesson you will understand why explicit versioning and clear visibility are vital, and you'll be ready to write and deploy a minimal contract locally. Consider: how does the constraint that every change costs gas change the way you design a function?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Solidity programs become immutable, gas-priced rules on the EVM. Begin with explicit compiler versions, a clear contract structure, and awareness of on-chain state and costs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain where Solidity fits in the Ethereum stack and write a minimal contract that stores and returns a value. Specifically, you'll learn to declare the compiler version so your code compiles predictably, to structure a contract with state variables and functions, and to use a constructor to set initial state. You'll also be introduced to basic value types such as unsigned integers and addresses which are essential for managing balances and identities. Each objective maps to a skill: reading and writing Solidity syntax, reasoning about on-chain persistence, and deploying a small contract in a local environment. These are practical skills: knowing how to pin a compiler version avoids wasted debugging when language features change, and understanding visibility prevents accidentally exposing internal data. We'll provide competency checks and small practice tasks so you can confirm your code compiles and behaves as expected. Think about a case where a constructor sets an administrator address — that pattern will appear in the hands-on activity.

keyIdea.title: Learning focus
keyIdea.text: Practice compiler versioning, contract structure, state variables, and basic types so you can deploy a simple contract locally with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.subtitle: Skills, pitfalls, and practical checks you will perform

narration.text: Beyond writing code, you will practice identifying common beginner pitfalls and confirming correct behavior. You will learn to spot deprecated constructor syntax, explicitly declare visibility on variables and functions, and reason about when a function should be declared 'view' to avoid unnecessary gas costs. A practical skill is to run a quick compilation check after adding a pragma and before deployment; this saves time and avoids subtle runtime surprises. We will also introduce basic value types like uint and address and discuss why the EVM's native word size makes uint256 a common choice. Finally, you'll perform an activity where you implement a simple counter contract and interact with increment and decrement functions on a local VM. These checks reinforce that smart contract development is both syntactic and behavioral: code must compile and also behave correctly on-chain. As you progress, always ask whether a change requires a transaction and gas, and whether visibility is explicit — those two questions prevent many beginner mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Practical checks
keyIdea.text: Compile early, set explicit visibility, prefer explicit constructor syntax, and verify whether functions are read-only to save gas.

screens.title: What is Solidity?
screens.subtitle: A contract-oriented language for the Ethereum Virtual Machine

narration.text: Solidity is a high-level, contract-oriented programming language designed specifically for writing smart contracts that run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine. That phrase 'contract-oriented' means the language is built to express rules, state, and interactions in a way that maps naturally to accounts, tokens, and workflows executed on a decentralized network. Solidity is statically typed, supports inheritance and libraries, and lets you define both basic and user-defined types. Being statically typed helps the compiler catch many errors before deployment, but it also requires you to be explicit about types and visibility. An important practical consequence is that Solidity code executes in a networked, resource-constrained environment where each operation has a gas cost. For example, updating a state variable in a contract is not free — it consumes gas and becomes part of the immutable on-chain state. A common misconception is to assume smart contract development is the same as server-side programming; it isn't. In servers you can patch or roll back code; on-chain code is effectively permanent once deployed. To ground this, imagine a simple escrow contract that holds funds until conditions are met; Solidity expresses the state-machine and enforcement rules, and those rules run on the EVM under gas accounting. Do you see how thinking about gas and immutability would change how you write even a single function?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Solidity expresses on-chain rules and state. Its static types and EVM execution model shape how you design secure, gas-efficient contracts.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Solidity?
A contract-oriented language for expressing on-chain rules and state on the EVM.
Core traits
  • Statically typed with explicit visibility
  • Supports inheritance and libraries
  • Designed to run under gas costs on the EVM
Analogy
Think of a Solidity contract as a small, public program and database that anyone can call; once deployed, its behavior and stored data are visible and persistent.
Why this matters
Design choices in Solidity directly affect cost and safety. For example, heavy data writes increase gas and permanently alter state. Small, efficient functions and explicit access control reduce risk.
Example scenario
A token transfer function that writes recipient balance will consume gas and permanently change balances on-chain, unlike in a centralized database where changes can be rolled back.
Key Takeaway

Solidity is purpose-built for secure, gas-aware, and persistent on-chain programs. Treat each operation as an irreversible, costed action.

screens.title: The pragma directive
screens.subtitle: Why pinning a compiler version matters

narration.text: Every Solidity file typically begins with a pragma directive that tells the compiler which versions of Solidity the source is compatible with. A common form is 'pragma solidity ^0.8.0;' which means the code should compile with any 0.8. x compiler starting at 0.8.0 but excluding 0.9.0. This is important because Solidity evolves and large changes can alter semantics and available features between major releases. If you omit a pragma or use a range that doesn't match the compiler, your code may fail to compile or behave differently at runtime. For example, constructor syntax changed historically and relying on older semantics can produce subtle bugs. Explicitly pinning a version or a compatible range is a lightweight insurance policy. A misconception is that the pragma enforces runtime behavior or gas limits; it does not. It only informs compilation compatibility. In practice, always set a pragma that matches the toolchain or environment you plan to use and test compilation on the same compiler version you will use for deployment. This small step prevents many frustrating compatibility issues. The pragma directive means pragma declares compiler compatibility. pin it to avoid breaking changes and to ensure predictable compilation and behavior.. In practical terms, why pinning a compiler version matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pragma purpose
keyIdea.text: Pragma declares compiler compatibility. Pin it to avoid breaking changes and to ensure predictable compilation and behavior.

content.html:
Definition
The pragma directive
Declare compiler version compatibility to avoid unexpected compilation or behavior changes.
Example declaration
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;
Use a pinned or compatible range matching your compiler toolchain. Testing on the same compiler version you plan to deploy with prevents compatibility surprises.
Why this matters
Compiler versions can change language semantics. Pinning prevents accidental use of deprecated or changed behaviors, such as constructor naming or ABI encoding updates.
Common misconception
Pragma does not set gas usage or runtime limits; it only constrains compiler selection for predictable source translation.
Key Takeaway

Set a clear pragma to protect your code from breaking changes and to ensure you compile with the intended Solidity version.

screens.title: Contract keyword and basic structure
screens.subtitle: Contracts as containers for state and functions

narration.text: The fundamental building block in Solidity is the contract, declared with the 'contract' keyword followed by its name and a code block. Conceptually it's similar to a class: it encapsulates state variables that persist on-chain and functions that operate on that state. A typical contract file begins with a pragma, then optional imports or libraries, and then one or more contract definitions. Inside a contract you'll find state variables, functions, events, and modifiers. State variables occupy storage that persists across transactions; functions can read or modify that storage. Naming and organizing contracts matters for readability, security and upgrade patterns. A common mistake is to put too much logic into a single contract without clear boundaries; consider separating responsibilities with libraries or multiple contracts when complexity grows. To make this concrete, imagine a simple contract that holds a message string and exposes functions to set and get it. The contract defines who can change the message and what reading it costs. When designing structure, think about access control, storage layout, and which functions should be 'view' only to avoid unnecessary transactions.

keyIdea.title: Contract structure
keyIdea.text: A contract encapsulates state and behavior. Organize code with clear responsibilities and explicit visibility for safety and clarity.

content.html:
Structure
Contract anatomy
Pragma → Imports → contract Name → state variables → constructor → functions
State variables
Persisted values stored in contract storage and visible on-chain depending on visibility.
Functions
Methods to read or modify state. Visibility and mutability determine how they execute and whether they cost gas.
Constructor
Runs once on deployment to set initial state, such as an owner or initial message.
Example contract outline
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Example {
  string public message; // state

  constructor(string memory initial) {
    message = initial; // initialized on deploy
  }

  function setMessage(string memory newMessage) public {
    message = newMessage; // modifies state
  }

  function getMessage() public view returns (string memory) {
    return message; // reads state without gas when called locally
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Contracts organize on-chain state and behavior. Keep responsibilities clear and set explicit visibility to match intended access.

screens.title: State variables and visibility
screens.subtitle: How state is stored and why visibility matters

narration.text: State variables are the persistent data members of a contract and they live in contract storage on the blockchain. When you declare a variable like 'uint public myNumber;', it is stored in persistent storage and the 'public' keyword automatically creates a read accessor. This is powerful but requires discipline: visibility modifiers — public, private, internal, external — control who can read or call your variables and functions, and default visibility can be surprising. For example, leaving visibility unspecified might expose data unintentionally. Storage operations are also expensive in gas compared to memory operations and only change when a transaction modifies state. A common beginner mistake is to assume local function variables behave like storage; they do not. Reference types such as arrays and structs default to storage or memory depending on context, but we will explore reference types in depth later. For now, focus on basic value types and making visibility explicit. A concrete example: a public 'message' string will generate a getter you can call without sending a transaction, while calling 'setMessage' to change it requires a transaction and consumes gas. As a takeaway, always declare visibility explicitly and consider who should be allowed to modify state.

keyIdea.title: State rules
keyIdea.text: State variables persist on-chain; explicit visibility prevents accidental exposure and distinguishes read-only access from state-changing transactions.

content.html:
State & Visibility
State variables
Persisted in contract storage and saved across transactions.
uint public myNumber;
string public message;
address owner;
Note that 'public' creates a getter. 'owner' without a visibility is internal by default in some contexts, so always declare it explicitly.
Example: public getter vs state change
Calling a generated getter for a public variable does not change state and can be read without a transaction. Invoking a setter that writes to storage requires a transaction and gas.
Common mistake
Assuming local variables are stored permanently or omitting visibility and relying on defaults. Always declare visibility and understand the storage vs memory context for reference types.
Key Takeaway

Declare visibility explicitly and remember: reads can be free when using view or getters, writes cost gas and change on-chain state.

screens.title: Basic value types: uint, address, bool
screens.subtitle: Choosing appropriate fundamental types and common considerations

narration.text: Solidity provides basic value types that you will use to represent quantities, identities, and logical values. The unsigned integer type, expressed as 'uint' or 'uint256', represents non-negative whole numbers and is commonly used for counters, balances and timestamps. Because the EVM uses 256-bit words, 'uint256' is often the most natural and sometimes gas-optimal choice. 'address' is a 20-byte type used to store Ethereum account addresses, whether externally owned or other contracts; it is essential for transfers and identifying owners. 'bool' holds true or false and is useful for simple flags like paused status or authorization checks. When selecting a type, think about range and intent: using a small width like 'uint8' can save storage in tightly packed structs but might create extra conversion work. A common misconception is that 'address' can store arbitrary strings — it cannot; it is a fixed-size 20-byte value and specific functions exist to send Ether or call other contracts. In practice, picking the right type improves clarity, reduces bugs, and may improve gas efficiency for storage-heavy contracts. As a practice check, ask whether a variable will store identifiers, counts, or boolean flags, and choose 'address', 'uint', or 'bool' accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Type selection
keyIdea.text: Pick types that reflect intent: 'uint' for counts and balances, 'address' for identities, 'bool' for flags. Consider EVM word size and storage packing trade-offs.

content.html:
Comparison
uint / uint256
Unsigned integer for counts and balances. Default size aligns with the EVM word size.
Use for: counters, token balances, timestamps
address
A 20-byte value representing an Ethereum account or contract. Used for transfers and ownership checks.
Use for: owners, recipients, contract references
bool
Simple true/false flag. Useful for pause switches and binary checks.
Use for: isActive, isPaused, hasAccess
Practical considerations
  • Prefer uint256 by default due to EVM alignment unless packing is needed.
  • Do not treat address as a string; use address-specific operations.
  • Booleans can be packed but may complicate struct layout; think about gas when storing many small values.

narration.text: A constructor is a special function in Solidity that runs once during contract deployment to initialize state. You declare it with the 'constructor' keyword and often pass initial values such as an owner address or an initial message. Initializing state in the constructor is important because it establishes the contract's starting conditions and any privileged roles. For example, in the HelloWorld contract you will set the initial message so readers can call a view function immediately after deployment. Historically, Solidity used to name constructors after the contract, but modern Solidity requires the explicit 'constructor' keyword; using the old pattern is a common beginner mistake and will not compile on newer compilers. Another important point is that constructor arguments must be supplied during deployment and do not exist afterward, so plan what must be set at deploy time versus what can be changed later. From a security perspective, initializing owners and access controls in the constructor helps prevent orphaned contracts. As a quick process: write the constructor, compile with the pinned pragma, deploy to a local VM with the constructor arguments, then verify the initial state via generated getters or view functions.

keyIdea.title: Constructor role
keyIdea.text: Constructors run once at deployment to set initial state and roles. Use the explicit constructor keyword and supply required arguments at deploy time.

content.html:
Constructor
Constructor usage
Declare 'constructor' to initialize state on deployment and pass any required start values.
Example constructor
constructor(string memory initialMessage) {
  message = initialMessage;
}
Deployment checklist
Write constructor → compile with pragma → supply arguments on deploy → verify initial state with getters or view functions.

screens.title: Functions: view vs state-changing and visibility
screens.subtitle: How function types affect gas, callers, and testing

narration.text: Solidity functions come in different flavors. A function labeled 'view' promises not to modify contract state; calling it from off-chain tooling or a read-only RPC does not require a transaction and thus does not consume gas for the caller. By contrast, functions that change state require sending a transaction and paying gas, because they alter persistent storage. Visibility modifiers — public, external, internal, private — determine who may call the function. Public functions are callable both internally and externally, and external functions are slightly more efficient when called from outside the contract. When writing functions, think about who should be allowed to call them and whether the function should change state. A common beginner error is to label a function without 'view' when it only reads state; this leads to unnecessary transactions in some workflows. Another practical tip is to test view functions in a local VM to confirm return values, and to simulate transactions to check gas cost before deploying to a public testnet. For example, in the HelloWorld contract, 'getMessage' is view and returns the current string, while 'setMessage' changes storage and requires a transaction. Closing question: which functions in your design must be 'view' and which must be full transactions?

keyIdea.title: Function types
keyIdea.text: Declare 'view' for read-only functions to avoid transactions. Use visibility to restrict callers and reduce attack surface.

content.html:
Functions & Gas
View vs State-changing
'view' functions do not modify storage and can be called without transactions; state-changing functions require transactions and gas.
function getMessage() public view returns (string memory) {
  return message;
}

function setMessage(string memory newMessage) public {
  message = newMessage;
}
Visibility considerations
  • Public: callable internally and externally; auto-generates getters for state variables.
  • External: better for external calls, slightly cheaper when called externally.
  • Internal/private: restrict access to within the contract or inheritance chain.
Common mistake

Failing to mark a read-only function as 'view' or leaving visibility implicit can lead to unnecessary gas costs and unintended access.

screens.title: HelloWorld contract walkthrough & local deploy steps
screens.subtitle: Read, compile, and deploy a simple contract to a local VM

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal HelloWorld contract that stores a message, sets it during deployment, and provides set and get functions. The contract begins with a SPDX license line and a pragma declaration to pin the compiler. Inside the contract we define a public state variable 'message' of type string. The constructor accepts 'initialMessage' and assigns it to the state. 'setMessage' allows anyone to change the message by sending a transaction, which updates storage and consumes gas. 'getMessage' is declared 'view' and returns the message without modifying state. To deploy this locally, open your preferred development environment such as a JavaScript VM in an online IDE or Ganache: create the file, ensure the pragma matches the compiler, compile, supply the constructor string when deploying, and observe the initial message via the generated getter. Then call 'setMessage' with a new string and re-check the getter to confirm state has changed. A common oversight is forgetting to set visibility or using outdated constructor naming; both cause compilation or runtime confusion. After you practice this deploy cycle, ask: how would you change the contract to restrict who can call setMessage?

keyIdea.title: Hands-on example
keyIdea.text: HelloWorld demonstrates constructor initialization, public state, a view getter, and a state-changing setter—perfect for a first local deployment and observation of on-chain state changes.

content.html:
Example Walkthrough
HelloWorld contract (visual)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract HelloWorld {
    string public message; // A public state variable to store our message

    // The constructor function is executed only once when the contract is deployed.
    constructor(string memory initialMessage) {
        message = initialMessage;
    }

    // A public function to update the message.
    function setMessage(string memory newMessage) public {
        message = newMessage;
    }

    // A public function to retrieve the current message.
    function getMessage() public view returns (string memory) {
        return message;
    }
}
Local deploy steps
  1. Create a new file and paste the contract, ensuring the pragma matches your compiler.
  2. Compile using your environment's compiler set to the pinned version.
  3. Deploy to a local JavaScript VM or Ganache, providing the constructor string.
  4. Call the getter to confirm the initial message, then call setMessage and confirm the update.
Key Takeaway

Deploying locally and observing constructor initialization and state changes is the fastest way to build reliable intuition about on-chain behavior and gas implications.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should retain. First, Solidity is a statically typed, contract-oriented language for the EVM; design choices must account for gas, immutability, and on-chain persistence. Second, the pragma directive pins compiler compatibility and prevents surprises from language changes. Third, a contract encapsulates state and functions; state variables persist in storage and require transactions to change. Fourth, basic value types like uint, address, and bool map to common on-chain needs: counts, identities, and flags. Fifth, constructors run once at deployment to set initial state, and modern Solidity uses the explicit 'constructor' keyword. Finally, mark functions as 'view' when they only read state to avoid unnecessary transactions. Keep these points in mind as you write and deploy small contracts locally, and use explicit visibility and versioning to reduce bugs.

keyIdea.title: Memory anchor
keyIdea.text: Solidity's language features reflect on-chain realities: pin compilers, declare visibility, choose appropriate types, and separate read-only from state-changing functions.

content.html:
Key Concepts
Solidity
A contract-oriented language for expressing on-chain rules and state on the EVM.
pragma
Pins compiler compatibility to ensure predictable compilation and behavior.
Contract
Encapsulates state variables and functions; organizes on-chain behavior.
Summary takeaway
Pin versions, declare visibility explicitly, use correct types, and separate read-only functions from state-changing ones to write predictable and safer contracts.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you start coding, hold three quick reminders in mind. First, always add a pragma that matches your compiler to avoid compilation surprises. Second, state is persistent and costly to change — use view functions for reads and only perform writes when necessary. Third, choose types and visibility deliberately: uint for numbers, address for identities, bool for flags, and explicitly set public, private, or internal depending on who should access the member. These concise checks will save time and reduce common beginner errors as you move from writing your first HelloWorld contract to more complex DApps. After this, implement the SimpleCounter activity to practice applying these rules: initialize state, expose a view getter, and test state changes locally. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means pragma, visibility, and type choices are your fastest way to avoid simple but costly mistakes in smart contract development.. In practical terms, three compact reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Pragma, visibility, and type choices are your fastest way to avoid simple but costly mistakes in smart contract development.

content.html:
What to Remember

Match compiler versions to avoid compatibility issues.
State & view
Reads can be view; writes require transactions and gas.
Type & visibility
Choose appropriate types and explicit visibility to prevent errors.
